title: Nine paths through the hull.
summary: Follow the actual lower-section curves from stern to bow. Compare height, curvature and curvature rate across four nested sampling intervals.
heroAlt: Centreline height, signed curvature and curvature rate at four arc-length intervals
heroCaption: Centreline · 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mm intervals · original derived-Brep curves. Lower two plots use signed logarithmic scales, linear near zero.

sections.title: Distance along the curve matters
sections.text: A uniformly spaced X coordinate is not a uniformly spaced journey along a curved surface. This study follows true numerical arc length, starting at each lower path’s own aft end and increasing forward. The centreline and four offsets on each side reveal how the lower hull changes across its width. Each path has its own origin and total length; equal arc-length values on different paths are not necessarily the same hull station.

sections.title: Three views of the same path
sections.text: Height shows the profile. Signed curvature shows how it bends. Curvature rate shows how that bending changes along the path. The plots preserve separate curve pieces and gaps in derivative stencils that cross detected tangent or curvature jumps. There is no smoothing or fitted replacement. Large end-region values need geometric context, particularly near a steep tail or bow.

sections.title: Explore the other eight paths
sections.text: Open any port or starboard study below. All four sampling intervals are overlaid; close agreement can make traces appear as one line. The original annotated sheets also identify topology and feature-review context.

sections.title: Refinement is part of the evidence
sections.text: The initial arc-length inversion failed an independent audit and was rejected. The corrected process uses numerical length integration with safeguarded inversion. The source reports a maximum independent inversion error of approximately 9.49 × 10⁻⁸ mm. This is an algorithm check on the analysis curves, not a manufacturing tolerance.

sections.title: Which features remain under refinement?
sections.text: Six candidates met the study’s convergence rules. The chart compares each candidate’s curvature-rate magnitude with its own finest-grid estimate. Stable location, magnitude and stencil agreement were required. The archive separately records 32 curvature discontinuities where finite rate is undefined, 13 numerical-sensitivity cases and five unresolved magnitude or stencil-sensitivity cases.

sections.title: Put the numerical result back on the hull
sections.text: The six converged positions are shown on the sampled geometry. This gives the numerical traces a physical location for further review. Convergence does not establish that a feature is undesirable, nor does it demonstrate drag reduction or handling. The nine paths are a targeted investigation rather than an exhaustive surface survey.

changes: Nine three-part plots, a convergence comparison and a location map redrawn from the corrected source data. Original annotated sheets remain available. Invalid initial-inversion results are excluded.

title: Check the geometry behind the analysis.
summary: Before drawing conclusions from sections, compare the derived analysis representation against the native hull.
heroAlt: Native sample to derived Brep distances projected onto hull coordinates
heroCaption: Distances in micrometres · recorded native surface samples to closest points on the derived Brep · top projection may overlap samples.

sections.title: The design master stays authoritative
sections.text: The native SubD is the design reference. The NURBS/Brep representation was created for analytical sectioning, with optional extraordinary-vertex G1/G2 postprocessing disabled. It is a separate analysis representation, not a revised hull design.

sections.title: Compare at the surface, not the control cage
sections.text: The validation uses native limit-surface vertices and face-centre samples. Those are compared with closest points on the derived representation. The recorded maximum sampled distance is approximately 0.000594 mm, or 0.594 micrometres. The comparison is small relative to the 0.1 mm document tolerance, but no manufacturing acceptance threshold was supplied.

sections.title: Position agreement is only one check
sections.text: The derived Brep was valid and solid, with 792 faces, no naked edges and no nonmanifold edges. The report gives conditional suitability for analytical sectioning. Small sampled position differences do not prove exact agreement everywhere or equivalent tangent and curvature behaviour around extraordinary vertices.

sections.title: Follow through with section-level checks
sections.text: The later fairness archive also records mirrored-section differences along the hull. The plot shows the maximum sampled value at each station on a logarithmic scale. It describes a numerical comparison of sampled geometry, not a continuous symmetry certificate.

title: The tail is a three-dimensional question.
summary: Closely spaced transverse cuts and longitudinal profiles reveal the geometry around the tail and its lower turnover.
heroAlt: Overlaid tail transverse sections on equal axes
heroCaption: Tail-study station convention: percentage measured from the physical bow toward the stern. This differs from the general stern-to-bow R02 stationing.

sections.title: Look through the tail, not just at its silhouette
sections.text: The source cuts through the aft region at closely spaced planes. Overlaying the returned section branches exposes the changing lower surface, raised lateral geometry and tail termination. Equal Y/Z scales preserve proportions. The curves are numerical intersections of the validated derived Brep, not exact native SubD sections.

sections.title: Follow the lower profiles
sections.text: Longitudinal lower-envelope samples provide another view of the same region. Each line retains its source branch and R01 longitudinal coordinates. Together with the transverse cuts, they explain why a single rear view cannot define a hydrodynamic release line.

sections.title: A reference plane is not a redesign
sections.text: The tail investigation distinguished the physical aft extent from a candidate lower centreline turnover used to discuss stationing. A scalar reference plane describes where measurements start; it does not flatten the shaped stern, extend the hull or certify where water releases during operation. The archived recommendation belongs to that stage of the study.

sections.title: Keep the geometry and flow questions connected
sections.text: These drawings establish the geometry available for meshing and later flow investigation. Actual wetted extent, separation and spray require hydrodynamic evidence under stated conditions. The fixed-hull CFD commissioning record is a subsequent step, with its own convergence limitations.

title: A feature is not automatically a flaw.
summary: Nine regions connect numerical flags with section geometry, native topology and visual review.
heroAlt: Nine feature-review regions on the actual sampled hull
heroCaption: Source region positions on R02 section samples. Amber: R5 and R9 need intent confirmation. Region labels are investigation references, not defect labels.

sections.title: Give every flag a geometric context
sections.text: The review examined nine regions using nearby transverse and longitudinal sections, control topology, shaded views, zebra patterns and reflections. This turns a curvature flag into a question that can be checked in several ways. Proximity to an extraordinary vertex does not by itself establish the cause of a surface transition.

sections.title: Preserve recognisable design features
sections.text: The review provisionally preserves the clear tail, rail and nose architecture. These features can produce strong curvature changes while still belonging to the intended form. Numerical prominence alone is not a reason to smooth them away.

sections.title: Leave unresolved intent visible
sections.text: R5 and R9 remain questions for design intent and local progression. The refined arc-length work does not erase those questions: sampled-peak convergence and an independently observed higher-order transition are different observations. A location-sensitive peak is not proof that the underlying transition is imaginary.

sections.title: Read the original visual evidence
sections.text: The original review sheet brings together the local sections and native visual checks. The separate native fairness sheet provides broader shaded and zebra views. These are engineering inspection images; their stripe patterns are visual aids, not measured water flow.
